To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
oxygen uptake is related to work rate during cycle ergometer exercises.

the relationship between oxygen uptake and work rate during cycle ergometer testing is linear and that the slope of this relationship is constant for a given individual, independent of the starting work rate.

the relationship between the work rate and the oxygen uptake (VO2) during incremental exercise on a cycle ergometer can be described by a linear function, with the slope of the function (the work rate increment) being constant for each subject and independent of the initial work rate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a study of the effects of the exercise of a single muscle on the oxygen consumption of other muscles.
the relationship between oxygen uptake and exercise intensity.
the relationship between the work rate and oxygen uptake (VO2) during exercise on a bicycle ergometer.

the linear relationship between oxygen uptake (VO2) and work rate increment (WRI) is a function of the work rate increment, the duration of the WRI, the duration of exercise, the duration of recovery, and the time interval between work rate increments.
the oxygen uptake response to exercise is a function of the intensity of the exercise and the fitness level of the subject, but not the mode of exercise.
the oxygen uptake during exercise is a linear function of the work rate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the relationship between oxygen uptake and work rate is not constant and is not linear, and that it is not possible to define a single value for VO2max.
the linear relationship between the rate of oxygen consumption and the rate of work done on a bicycle ergometer is a result of the linear relationship between oxygen consumption and heart rate.
the linear increase of oxygen uptake with work rate is not an intrinsic property of the oxygen uptake-work rate relationship but a consequence of the linear increase in work rate.

oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production are not linearly correlated during exercise, even when the work rate is constant.
